notes.b: The Gaeltacht is the area where Irish is the community language. Its extent has shrunk as speakers have declined.
points: Census 1851, the first census to count Irish speakers: about 1.5 million Irish speakers, about 23% of the population. Irish-speaking areas then covered much of the west and south.
The Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration hit the poor, western, Irish-speaking areas hardest.
National schools, set up in 1831, taught through English.
English became the language of law, trade, politics, the Church and emigration. Parents saw English as the route to work.
Census 1891: about 680,000 Irish speakers, about 14% of the population.

notes.h: Revival and the first official Gaeltacht boundaries
points: The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge), founded in 1893 by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill, promoted the language.
The new state's language policy made Irish compulsory in schools and required for some public jobs.

Coimisiún na Gaeltachta reported in 1926 and defined two types of Gaeltacht. Fíor-Ghaeltacht ('true' Gaeltacht): districts where 80% or more spoke Irish. Breac-Ghaeltacht ('partly' Gaeltacht): districts with 25–79% Irish speakers.
The 1926 definitions covered a large area across many western and southern counties.
The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 shrank the official Gaeltacht to areas where Irish was still the community language.
The Department of the Gaeltacht (Roinn na Gaeltachta) was set up in 1956. Gaeltarra Éireann, the Gaeltacht industry body, followed in 1957. Later small extensions were made by order.
Gaeltacht areas lie in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.
The Meath Gaeltacht was built by planned colonies: Ráth Chairn, settled in 1935 by families moved from Connemara, and Baile Ghib, settled in 1937.
Galway (Conamara) has the largest Gaeltacht population; Donegal is second.
Census 2022: the Gaeltacht population was about 106,000, and about 20,000 Gaeltacht residents speak Irish daily outside the education system.
Nationally (Census 2022): about 1.87 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish; about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.

notes.h: State and community supports for Irish
points: Údarás na Gaeltachta, the Gaeltacht development authority, was set up in 1980 to replace Gaeltarra Éireann. The Gaoth Dobhair (Gweedore) industrial estate in Co. Donegal is an example of Gaeltacht industry.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting in 1972. TG4 (originally Teilifís na Gaeilge) launched on 31 October 1996.
The Official Languages Act 2003 (amended 2021) gives Irish official status.
Irish became an official EU language in 2007 and gained full working-language status on 1 January 2022.
The 20-Year Strategy for the Irish Language covers 2010 to 2030.
Gaeltacht summer colleges give young people intensive immersion in Irish.

notes.h: Gaeltacht Act 2012: boundaries defined by language
points: The Gaeltacht Act 2012 defined the Gaeltacht by language use rather than by a fixed map.
Gaeltacht Language Planning Areas: 26, each needing a language plan.
Gaeltacht Service Towns, and Irish Language Networks outside the Gaeltacht, extend Irish use beyond the core areas.
The Comprehensive Linguistic Study of the Use of Irish in the Gaeltacht (2007) found that Irish is viable as a community language only where at least 67% of people speak it daily.
Its 2015 update warned that Irish could cease to be the community language in most Gaeltacht districts within about ten years.
Pressures: in-migration of English speakers; suburban growth, such as Galway city's spread west; tourism; emigration of young people; English-language media.
Housing with language conditions, so that Irish speakers can afford to stay in Gaeltacht areas.
Jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta and Gaeltacht industry.
Irish-medium schooling and preschools.
Language plans in each Language Planning Area.
Family supports for Irish-speaking households, and Irish-language media such as TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.

notes.h: Belgium: a language border made official
notes.b: Belgium is a brief comparison: a language boundary fixed in law. Its present-day relations are in the s3 notes.
points: The language border between Dutch- and French-speaking areas was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963.
The first state reform came in 1970. Belgium became a federal state in 1993, with Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital as its regions.

notes.h: Dublin's suburban growth and the Greater Dublin Area
notes.b: Dublin's growth has spread from the city into the surrounding counties.
points: Suburban expansion from the 1950s and 1960s led to the Advisory Regional Plan for Dublin (Myles Wright, 1967), which proposed new towns west of the city: Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
Ballymun: seven 15-storey tower blocks built 1966–69 and demolished between 2004 and 2015 under a regeneration plan.
Census 2022: County Dublin had about 1.46 million people.
The Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population.
Commuter towns in the surrounding counties include Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge.

notes.h: Dublin council structures and regional authorities
points: Rathmines and Pembroke townships were added to Dublin city in 1930.

Local Government (Dublin) Act 1993: from 1 January 1994, Dublin County Council was replaced by Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Councils. The county had grown too large to govern as one unit, and local government needed to be closer to the people.
Dublin Corporation was renamed Dublin City Council in 2002 under the Local Government Act 2001.
Census 2022 populations of the four Dublin local authorities: Dublin City about 590,000; Fingal about 330,000; South Dublin about 300,000; Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown about 235,000.
The Dublin Regional Authority was set up in 1994.

The Local Government Reform Act 2014 replaced the regional authorities, including the Dublin Regional Authority, with three regional assemblies from 2015: Northern and Western; Eastern and Midland; Southern.

notes.h: Problems of an expanding city region and planning responses
points: Problems: urban sprawl, long commutes, congestion, housing costs, one-off housing and dormitory growth.

The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), published in 2018, aims for half of future population growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford) and to limit sprawl.
Transport: the M50 orbital motorway was built in stages from 1990, the Luas light rail opened in 2004, and DART serves the suburbs by rail.
Regeneration: the IFSC was set up in the Docklands in 1987; the Docklands and Ballymun are regeneration areas.
The Citizens' Assembly reported in 2023, recommending a directly elected mayor for Dublin.
Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor in June 2024, after a plebiscite in 2019.

notes.h: Other Irish boundary changes and economic regions
points: Cork city boundary extended on 31 May 2019, taking in suburbs such as Ballincollig, Glanmire and Blarney from the county.
Limerick City and County Council and Waterford City and County Council were formed by merger in 2014.
From 1999/2000 Ireland was divided for EU purposes into two NUTS 2 regions: the Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region, and the Southern and Eastern region.
The BMW region kept Objective 1 (poorest-region) funding status for 2000–06.
The economic regions were drawn for EU funding, so their boundaries follow economic need rather than language or identity.
Reasons: peace after two world wars; rebuilding after the war; coal and steel placed under shared control; economic growth; the Cold War.
Schuman Declaration, 9 May 1950 (now Europe Day), proposed pooling coal and steel production.
The Treaty of Paris (1951) set up the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC).
The Treaty of Rome (1957, in force 1958) set up the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom.
The six founders ('the Six') were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

notes.b: Dates only. The issues raised by each step are in the s3 notes.
points: Single European Act: 1986, in force 1987.
Single market: from 1 January 1993.
Maastricht Treaty: signed 7 February 1992; in force 1 November 1993, creating the European Union.
Euro: launched 1 January 1999 for banks and electronic payments; notes and coins from 1 January 2002.
Lisbon Treaty: in force 1 December 2009.
1973: Ireland, the UK and Denmark. 1981: Greece. 1986: Spain and Portugal.
1990: East Germany joined through reunification with West Germany.
1995: Austria, Finland and Sweden.
2004: ten countries joined: Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
2007: Bulgaria and Romania. 2013: Croatia, the most recent member.
The UK left on 31 January 2020, leaving 27 members with about 450 million people (2024).
The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, opening the way for former communist states to seek EU membership.

Copenhagen criteria (1993): stable democracy, rule of law, human rights and protection of minorities; a working market economy able to cope with competition; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership.
Most of the 2004 entrants, and both 2007 entrants, were former communist states.
Effects on newer members: economic growth, EU funds and emigration.
Effects on older members: competition for jobs and investment, and migration from the newer members.
Croatia joined the Schengen area in 2023. Bulgaria and Romania joined it fully on 1 January 2025.
In 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to give the new members' citizens immediate access to their labour markets.
Polish was the most common language other than English and Irish spoken at home in Census 2016 and Census 2022.
Advantages: a larger market; a labour supply for the Celtic Tiger economy; cultural diversity; export opportunities.
Disadvantages: competition for foreign direct investment from lower-cost states; less EU regional funding for Ireland; pressure on wages and services.
Example of investment competition: Dell announced in January 2009 that it would move its manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.

notes.h: Future expansion: benefits to the EU and candidates
notes.b: The current candidate countries are named in the s3 notes.
points: Benefits of further expansion for the EU: a larger single market with more consumers, and greater stability on its borders.
Benefits for candidates: access to the single market and to EU funding, and reforms to meet the Copenhagen criteria.

notes.b: Partition of Ireland redrew a political boundary across a single island. Its present-day effects, including the Good Friday Agreement and Brexit, are in the s3 notes.
points: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned the island. Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six of Ulster's nine counties.
Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan went to the Irish Free State.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in December 1921.
Boundary Commission (1925): its report was not published, and the border was left unchanged.
The border created a nationalist minority in the north and a small Protestant minority in the south.
Impact: nationalists in Northern Ireland faced discrimination, which fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968 and then the Troubles.
Communities, parishes and farms were divided by the border.
Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic federal state. Its new borders followed the old internal republic lines, leaving Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities on the 'wrong' side of them.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991; Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in 1992.
War and ethnic cleansing followed in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Srebrenica, July 1995: about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces.
The Dayton Agreement (1995) divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.
Montenegro became independent in 2006. Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008; Serbia does not recognise it.
In 1945 Poland's western border moved to the Oder–Neisse line. The USSR took Poland's eastern lands.
Millions of Germans were expelled westwards, and Poles were resettled from the east.
The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, dividing Germany and Berlin.
Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.

notes.h: Break-up of the USSR and Czechoslovakia
points: The USSR broke up in 1991 into 15 independent states.
Ethnic Russians became minorities in newly independent states. In Estonia and Latvia they make up roughly a fifth to a quarter of the population.
Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the 'Velvet Divorce'.

notes.h: Cyprus: a divided island in the EU
points: The Turkish invasion of July 1974 divided Cyprus between Greek Cypriots in the south and Turkish Cypriots in the north.
The UN buffer zone, the Green Line, runs through Nicosia.
The 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' is recognised only by Turkey.
2004 Annan Plan referendum: about 65% of Turkish Cypriots voted Yes, and about 76% of Greek Cypriots voted No.
Cyprus joined the EU in 2004, but EU law is suspended in the north.

notes.b: A non-European example of a political boundary redrawn along religious lines.
points: Partition of India, August 1947: India and Pakistan (including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) were created along religious lines.
Around 15 million people were displaced, and hundreds of thousands were killed in communal violence.

notes.h: General conclusions on boundaries and cultural groups
points: Boundaries drawn across cultural groups create minorities, displacement and conflict.
Boundaries drawn around cultural groups, as in Belgium, can reduce conflict but can harden division.
Shared institutions, such as power-sharing and EU membership, can soften the effect of a border.

keyTerms.definition: The areas where Irish is the community language; since 2012 defined by language use.
Districts where 80% or more of people spoke Irish, as defined by the 1926 Commission.
Districts with 25–79% Irish speakers, as defined by the 1926 Commission.
One of the 26 areas under the Gaeltacht Act 2012, each needing a language plan.
The first Irish census to count Irish speakers, showing about 23% of the population spoke Irish.
The admission of new member states to the EU, as in 1973, 1981, 1986, 1995, 2004, 2007 and 2013.
The 1993 conditions a candidate must meet to join the EU: stable democracy, a working market economy and the ability to take on membership obligations.
Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, a city region of about 2.1 million people in Census 2022.
A county, city or town council responsible for local government in its area.
EU funding status for the poorest regions, held by the Border, Midland and Western region for 2000–06.
The division of a territory into separate states, as with Ireland in 1921 and India in 1947.
One of the two constituent parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Dayton Agreement.
A neutral strip between opposing forces, such as the Green Line through Nicosia.

factCards.term: Irish speakers 1851 to 1891, and why the language declined
factCards.definition: Census 1851: about 1.5 million Irish speakers (23%); 1891: about 680,000 (14%). Causes: the Famine (1845–49) and emigration hit poor western Irish-speaking areas hardest; national schools (1831) taught through English; English was the language of law, trade and emigration.

factCards.term: Gaeltacht boundaries: how they were drawn and redrawn, 1926 to 2012
factCards.definition: 1926: Coimisiún na Gaeltachta drew a large Gaeltacht across many western and southern counties. 1956: the Gaeltacht Areas Order shrank it to where Irish was still the community language. 2012: the Gaeltacht Act based it on language use, with 26 Language Planning Areas.

factCards.term: Supports for the Irish language and the Gaeltacht since 1893
factCards.definition: Gaelic League (1893, Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill); Department of the Gaeltacht (1956); Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980), e.g. Gaoth Dobhair estate; Raidió na Gaeltachta (1972); TG4 (1996); Official Languages Act 2003; full EU working language (2022); 20-Year Strategy 2010–2030.

factCards.term: The Gaeltacht today: counties and Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: Seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath (colonies at Ráth Chairn, 1935, and Baile Ghib, 1937). Galway has the largest Gaeltacht population, then Donegal. Census 2022: about 106,000 people, about 20,000 speaking Irish daily outside education.

factCards.term: Continuing decline of Irish in the Gaeltacht: evidence and pressures
factCards.definition: The 2007 study found Irish survives as a community language only where 67% or more speak it daily; its 2015 update warned most districts could lose it within about ten years. Pressures: in-migrants who speak English, Galway's spread west, tourism, youth emigration.

factCards.term: Strategies to address the decline of Irish in the Gaeltacht
factCards.definition: Housing with language conditions; jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta; Irish-medium schools and preschools; a language plan for each Language Planning Area; family supports and Irish-language media such as TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.

factCards.term: Belgium: how a language boundary was made official
factCards.definition: The border between Dutch- and French-speaking areas was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963. The first state reform came in 1970, and Belgium became a federal state in 1993, with three regions: Flanders, Wallonia and bilingual Brussels-Capital.

factCards.term: Dublin's urban growth and the Greater Dublin Area
factCards.definition: Myles Wright's plan (1967) proposed new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown. Ballymun's seven 15-storey towers (1966–69) were demolished 2004–2015. Census 2022: County Dublin about 1.46 million; Greater Dublin Area about 2.1 million (about 40%).

factCards.term: Dublin council structures: how and why they changed
factCards.definition: Rathmines and Pembroke were added to the city in 1930. On 1 January 1994 Dublin County Council was split into Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, because the county was too big to govern as one; Dublin Corporation became Dublin City Council in 2002.

factCards.term: Regional assemblies and other Irish boundary changes
factCards.definition: In 2015 the Dublin Regional Authority (1994) was replaced by the Eastern and Midland Regional Assembly, one of three (with Northern and Western, and Southern). Limerick and Waterford city and county councils merged (2014); Cork city took in Ballincollig, Glanmire and Blarney (31 May 2019).

factCards.term: Dublin city region: problems and planning responses
factCards.definition: Problems: sprawl, long commutes, congestion, housing costs, dormitory towns. Responses: National Planning Framework (2018), half of growth in five cities; M50 (from 1990), Luas (2004), DART; Docklands and Ballymun regeneration; a directly elected mayor recommended in 2023.

factCards.term: Origins of the EU: reasons and founding steps
factCards.definition: Reasons: peace after two world wars, rebuilding, shared control of coal and steel, growth, the Cold War. Schuman Declaration (9 May 1950); ECSC (1951); EEC and Euratom (Treaty of Rome, 1957). The Six: Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands.

factCards.term: Deepening of the EU: key treaty and market dates
factCards.definition: Single European Act 1986; single market from 1 January 1993; Maastricht Treaty signed 7 February 1992, creating the EU (in force 1 November 1993); euro 1999, with notes and coins in 2002; Lisbon Treaty in force 1 December 2009.

factCards.term: EU enlargement, 1973 to 1995: who joined when
factCards.definition: 1973: Ireland, the UK and Denmark. 1981: Greece. 1986: Spain and Portugal. 1990: East Germany, through German reunification. 1995: Austria, Finland and Sweden.

factCards.term: EU enlargement since 2004: who joined, and who left
factCards.definition: 2004: Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia. 2007: Bulgaria and Romania. 2013: Croatia, the most recent member. The UK left on 31 January 2020, leaving 27 members.

factCards.term: Eastern European expansion: background and effects
factCards.definition: After the Berlin Wall fell (9 November 1989), ex-communist states sought entry under the Copenhagen criteria (1993); most 2004 entrants and both 2007 entrants were ex-communist. New members gained growth and EU funds but lost emigrants; older members faced competition.

factCards.term: Impact of EU enlargement on Ireland: advantages and disadvantages
factCards.definition: Advantages: a larger market; workers for the Celtic Tiger (Ireland opened its labour market at once in 2004); diversity, with Polish the main other home language. Disadvantages: competition for FDI (Dell to Łódź, 2009); less EU regional funding; pressure on services.

factCards.term: Benefits of further EU expansion
factCards.definition: For the EU: a larger single market with more consumers, and greater stability on its borders. For candidate countries: access to the single market and EU funding, and reforms to meet the Copenhagen criteria.

factCards.term: Partition of Ireland: how the border was drawn
factCards.definition: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned the island; Northern Ireland (1921) took six of Ulster's nine counties, leaving Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan to the Free State. The Anglo-Irish Treaty followed (1921); the Boundary Commission (1925) left the border unchanged.

factCards.term: Partition of Ireland: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: It left a nationalist minority in the north and a small Protestant minority in the south. Discrimination against northern nationalists fuelled the civil rights movement (1968) and the Troubles (over 3,500 killed); the border divided communities, parishes and farms.

factCards.term: Break-up of Yugoslavia: boundary changes and impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: Borders followed old republic lines, so the independence of Slovenia and Croatia (1991) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992) stranded Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities. War and ethnic cleansing followed: Srebrenica (July 1995, about 8,000 killed); Dayton (1995) split Bosnia in two.

factCards.term: Post-war Poland and Germany: boundary changes and their impact
factCards.definition: In 1945 Poland's western border moved to the Oder–Neisse line and the USSR took its eastern lands; millions of Germans were expelled westwards and Poles resettled from the east. Germany was divided (Berlin Wall 1961–1989) and reunified on 3 October 1990.

factCards.term: Break-up of the USSR and Czechoslovakia: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: The USSR split into 15 states in 1991, leaving ethnic Russians as minorities, about a fifth to a quarter of the people in Estonia and Latvia. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993: the Velvet Divorce.

factCards.term: Cyprus: a divided island inside the EU
factCards.definition: Divided since the Turkish invasion of July 1974, with the UN Green Line through Nicosia; only Turkey recognises the north. In the 2004 Annan Plan vote about 65% of Turkish Cypriots said Yes, 76% of Greek Cypriots No. Cyprus joined the EU in 2004; EU law is suspended in the north.

factCards.term: Partition of India, 1947: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: In August 1947 India and Pakistan (including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) were created along religious lines; around 15 million people were displaced and hundreds of thousands were killed in communal violence.

questions.prompt: Changes in political boundaries can impact on cultural groups. Examine this statement with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Partition of Ireland: the Government of Ireland Act (1920) and Northern Ireland's creation in 1921 with six of Ulster's nine counties left a nationalist minority in the north and a small Protestant minority in the south. The Boundary Commission (1925) left the border unchanged. Nationalists faced discrimination, which fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968 and then the Troubles. Communities, parishes and farms were divided. Break-up of Yugoslavia: a multi-ethnic federal state whose new borders followed its internal republic lines, leaving Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities on the wrong side. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991 and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. War and ethnic cleansing followed, including the killing of about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995. The Dayton Agreement (1995) divided Bosnia into two entities. Montenegro became independent in 2006 and Kosovo in 2008. Conclusion: boundaries drawn across cultural groups create minorities, displacement and conflict; boundaries drawn around groups, as in Belgium, can reduce conflict but harden division; shared institutions can soften a border's effect.

Official boundaries: the 1926 Commission defined Fíor-Ghaeltacht (80% or more speakers) and Breac-Ghaeltacht (25–79%), covering a large area across many western and southern counties. The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 shrank the official Gaeltacht to areas where Irish was still the community language, and the Department of the Gaeltacht was set up that year. The 2007 study found Irish viable as a community language only where at least 67% speak it daily, and its 2015 update warned of decline within about ten years. Pressures include in-migration, suburban growth, tourism, emigration of young people and English-language media. Strategies include language housing conditions, jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta, Irish-medium schooling and language plans.

questions.prompt: (i) Name two countries that have joined the EU since Ireland joined in 1973. (ii) Explain the advantages of EU expansion for Ireland. (iii) Explain the disadvantages.
questions.model: (i) Any two of: Greece (1981), Spain and Portugal (1986), Austria, Finland and Sweden (1995), Poland, Hungary and the other 2004 entrants, Bulgaria and Romania (2007), Croatia (2013). (ii) Advantages: a larger market for Irish exports and more export opportunities; a labour supply that helped sustain the Celtic Tiger economy; cultural diversity from new members' citizens, such as the Polish community, which is the largest after English and Irish at home (Census 2016 and 2022). Ireland, the UK and Sweden gave the 2004 entrants immediate access to their labour markets. (iii) Disadvantages: competition for foreign direct investment from lower-cost states, as when Dell moved its manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, in 2009 with the loss of about 1,900 jobs; less EU regional funding for Ireland; pressure on wages and services as workers arrive from the newer members.
